      Featured Article: Margin Coverage Option Amid Cost Disruptions

      Crop insurance has traditionally focused on protecting producers against losses in yield and revenue, but it offers much less protection when pressure comes from the cost side of the farm margin. That distinction became especially important in 2026, when conflict in the Middle East disrupted fertilizer and energy markets and sharply increased the prices of several major farm inputs. As a result, producers faced a direct compression of operating margins, creating an early test for the Margin Coverage Option (MCO), a supplemental crop insurance endorsement introduced for the 2026 crop year.

      MCO is designed to protect county-level operating margins rather than revenue alone. It can respond to lower crop prices, lower yields, higher input costs, or some combination of the three. [See details at https://www.rma.usda.gov/policy-procedure/general-policies/margin-coverage-option.] For producers who purchased MCO for 2026, the timing of the conflict was particularly important because projected input prices had been established the previous fall, while final MCO input prices were determined in April after fertilizer and energy markets had been disrupted. The resulting increase in indexed production costs reduced insured margins and raised the likelihood of MCO payments. Final indemnities will still depend on harvest crop prices and county yields, but current market conditions provide a useful illustration of how margin coverage can respond to risks that conventional revenue products do not directly insure.

      The 2026 Hormuz Disruption

      In early March 2026, commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted. Major Protection and Indemnity clubs subsequently suspended war-risk coverage, effectively halting commercial transit through the Strait (Arita et al., 2026). The implications for agricultural input markets were significant because the Gulf is a major supplier of fertilizer and energy products. In 2024, the region accounted for 43 percent of global urea exports and 44 percent of sulfur trade, and unlike Russian supplies during the 2022 disruption, Gulf production has no viable alternative export route when the Strait is closed (Arita et al., 2026). Within three weeks, urea spot prices had risen 28.2 percent, diammonium phosphate (DAP) 2.6 percent, and farm diesel 34.7 percent (Chakravorty et al., 2026; Arita et al., 2026).

      The effect on crop prices was much smaller. The Persian Gulf imports rather than exports grain, so the disruption did not remove large quantities of grain from world markets (Arita et al., 2026; Arita et al., 2026). Corn prices rose only 3.6 percent in the weeks following the closure, while soybean prices declined slightly (Chakravorty et al., 2026). The result was a cost shock that had relatively little revenue-side offset immediately after the conflict. This distinction matters for crop insurance because a revenue policy may provide protection when yields or crop prices fall, but it does not directly compensate a producer simply because fertilizer, fuel, or other production costs increase. MCO was designed to address part of that exposure.

      How MCO Works

      MCO is an area-based crop insurance endorsement introduced by RMA for crop year 2026. Instead of insuring revenue alone, it protects an indexed operating margin constructed from county revenue and selected production costs. Revenue is based on county yields and futures-based crop prices, while the cost component uses RMA-specified input quantities and futures-based prices for urea, DAP, potash, diesel, and natural gas. Natural gas is included only for irrigated practices. [Futures contract months vary by location.] This structure allows changes in selected input prices to directly affect the insured margin rather than operating only indirectly through farm profitability.

      The price-discovery schedule is central to how the product responds to cost shocks. For most crops, projected crop and input prices are established from August 15 through September 15 before the insured crop year. Final crop prices generally follow the harvest price discovery periods used for traditional COMBO products, while final input prices are determined from average futures prices during April 1 through April 30. A cost shock occurring after fall enrollment but before April can therefore reduce the final insured margin even if yields and crop prices remain relatively stable. If input prices rise and crop revenue does not increase enough to compensate, the likelihood of an MCO payment increases.

      For crop year 2026, MCO was available for corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, sorghum, and rice. [Offerings closely matched the geographical distribution of what is currently offered for Margin Protection.] The coverage band extends from either 95 or 90 percent down to 86 percent, and MCO must be purchased as an endorsement to an underlying individual policy such as Yield Protection, Revenue Protection, Revenue Protection with Harvest Price Exclusion, or Actual Production History. MCO can be combined with SCO but not ECO because the MCO and ECO coverage bands overlap. Following the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the subsidy rate increased to 80 percent, matching the subsidy rates for ECO, SCO, and STAX. [See https://www.rma.usda.gov/policy-procedure/bulletins-memos/managers-bulletin/mgr-25-006-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-amendment.] These design features make MCO a direct alternative to ECO for producers deciding how to insure the upper part of their risk exposure.

      First-Year Adoption Remains Limited

      As of September 16, 2026, data from the RMA Summary of Business show limited MCO adoption for crop year 2026. A total of 8,959 MCO policies were sold, with 99.4 percent at the 95 percent coverage level. Endorsed acreage remains preliminary while acreage reporting continues, so policy counts provide the cleaner measure of early adoption. By comparison, ECO had 533,498 policies sold on the same basis, meaning MCO represented approximately 1.7 percent of the combined MCO and ECO policy pool. The low first-year adoption is important when interpreting the 2026 shock because MCO may prove valuable for producers who purchased it, but relatively few producers entered the year with that protection.

      First-year MCO participation is concentrated rather than broadly distributed across eligible crops: soybeans and corn alone account for more than 90 percent of policies sold (Table 4). Cotton sales were concentrated in Texas and Oklahoma, grain sorghum sales in Texas and Kansas, and spring wheat policies primarily in North Dakota and Minnesota. The geographic concentration also matters for the simulations below because current estimates describe the counties in which producers actually enrolled rather than the full set of counties where MCO was available.

      The Cost Shock Moved Directly Into MCO Margins

      MCO final input prices are set as average futures prices during April. Because the effects of the conflict extended throughout this price discovery period, the shock carried directly into the 2026 MCO cost calculation. Table 5 reports the projected and final prices for the inputs included in the MCO index. Relative to projected prices set the previous fall, urea increased 65.3 percent, DAP increased 9.9 percent, diesel increased 79.8 percent, potash increased 30.8 percent, and natural gas decreased 22.8 percent. The movements represent a substantial shift in the cost component of the MCO margin within a single crop year.

      The magnitude of the 2026 increases is also notable in historical context. We compare the 2026 projected-to-final price changes with equivalent changes since 2016, calculated as though MCO had existed in those earlier years. Urea recorded its largest increase over that period in 2026. The increases in other fertilizers and diesel were also substantial, although generally below the spikes observed around 2021 and 2022. Figure 17 places the 2026 price changes alongside these historical movements and shows that the current episode ranks among the more consequential cost shocks of the past decade.

      Figure 17. Historical Changes in Input Prices Between Projected and Harvest Price Discovery Periods.

      Note: Harvest prices are set in April and projected prices are set in the previous August–September period. Rice has a different discovery period.

      Source: NDSU Agricultural Risk Policy Center (ARPC) using data from Bloomberg and the MCO and MP Price Discovery Tools, as of September 16, 2026.

      Higher input prices translated into higher MCO-indexed production costs across covered commodities. These are not farm-specific production expenses, but index costs calculated using RMA-defined input quantities tied to expected county yields and futures-based fertilizer and energy prices. Figure 18 shows how indexed costs changed between the projected and final price discovery periods and how the 2026 changes compare with previous years. On average, MCO-indexed costs increased sharply in 2026 and rank among the largest increases since 2016. This matters because higher indexed costs reduce the final county margin even if crop prices and yields remain unchanged.

      MCO payments are triggered when final county-level margins fall below the trigger margin, which is based on expected revenue, expected costs, and the selected coverage level. When MCO is paired with Revenue Protection, the calculation can also reflect the harvest price option because the revenue guarantee may increase when the harvest crop price exceeds the projected price. The final effect therefore depends on the interaction of crop prices, county yields, and indexed input costs rather than input prices alone. Nevertheless, the input price movements have increased the probability of MCO triggering a payment.

      What Current Conditions Imply for 2026 Payments

      Final MCO input prices are now known, but final indemnities are not. Harvest crop prices will be established in October for most crops, and 2026 county yields are expected to become available from RMA in 2027. The estimates presented here should therefore be interpreted as forward-looking values under current market conditions rather than final indemnity estimates. To examine current exposure, we use a simulation framework based on market conditions as of September 10, 2026, RMA expected county yields, historical yield variability, and RMA-implied price-yield correlations. The analysis focuses on MCO-95 corn and soybean policies in counties with reported enrollment.

      The results indicate that MCO-95 has become a meaningful exposure rather than a remote layer of coverage for enrolled counties. Figure 19 shows that the estimated probability of triggering a corn payment averages about 55 percent, with the highest probabilities concentrated across the core Corn Belt. Soybean trigger probabilities are lower and geographically more uniform, averaging about 45 percent across enrolled counties. These probabilities reflect current market conditions together with county expected yields, yield variability, price-yield relationships, and the structure of the MCO coverage band. They are lower than the same simulation run on June 30 conditions, which put the corn average near 77 percent and the soybean average near 64 percent. The decline follows from the projected prices used in each run rather than from any easing of the cost shock: higher expected crop prices raise expected revenue and therefore the expected margin, which moves the margin away from the trigger. Even after that decline, the probabilities show how strongly the cost shock has moved the insured margin before final crop prices and county yields are known.

      Figure 19. Estimated Probability of Triggering a Margin Coverage Option (MCO-95) Payment for Non-Irrigated Corn and Soybeans, 2026.

      The cost shock also produces positive expected net returns for current MCO-95 policyholders. Figure 20 reports expected net return per acre and per dollar of liability, where expected net return is the simulated expected MCO-95 payment less the farm-paid premium. For corn, expected net returns average approximately $28.21 per acre after an average producer-paid premium of about $7.82 per acre. For soybeans, the corresponding expected net return is $15.35 per acre after an average producer-paid premium of about $5.07 per acre. Relative to insured liability, expected net returns average approximately 0.33 for corn and 0.24 for soybeans, allowing comparisons across counties.

      For corn, higher expected returns per acre are concentrated in Iowa, Illinois, and nearby Corn Belt counties. For soybeans, the highest per-acre returns are more concentrated in Iowa, Nebraska, and southern Minnesota, with lower values across parts of Illinois and North Dakota. Together, Figure 19 and Figure 20 show that the 2026 input cost shock has materially increased both the probability of an MCO payment and the expected value of that payment for currently enrolled producers. The geographic patterns reflect the interaction of county expected yields, RMA yield variability, price-yield correlations, input cost exposure, and the fixed MCO coverage band. Details of the simulation are presented in the supplementary note below.

      The estimates can still change materially before the crop year is complete. Weather-related yield shocks and events not currently priced into futures markets could alter both trigger probabilities and expected payments. The current results should therefore be viewed as a measure of exposure under the information available at this point in the season rather than a prediction of final indemnities. As harvest approaches and uncertainty narrows, the probability of triggering and expected net returns can be reassessed using updated crop prices and yield information.

      Protection Comes With Basis Risk

      The 2026 experience demonstrates the potential value of margin coverage, but an MCO payment should not be interpreted as a direct measure of an individual farm's change in profitability. MCO is an index product, so its margin can differ from the margin actually experienced by a producer through both yield basis risk and cost basis risk. Yield basis risk arises because an individual farm's yield is not perfectly correlated with the county-level yield used by MCO and ECO, reducing the degree to which county-based insurance matches farm-level losses (Monaco et al., 2026; Tsay and Paulson, 2024). A producer can experience a poor yield when the county does not, or the county can experience a loss that is not representative of a particular farm. This familiar source of basis risk remains present even though MCO adds a cost component to the insurance calculation.

      Cost basis risk adds another layer because both the quantity and price of inputs can differ between the MCO index and an individual operation. Farms use different combinations and quantities of fertilizer, fuel, and other inputs, so a producer using proportionally more of one input and less of another may experience a cost change that differs substantially from the index. The timing of purchases also matters because MCO uses futures prices from its August to September and April discovery periods, while actual farm expenses depend on when inputs are purchased. A producer who prepaid for urea or DAP before the conflict may therefore have incurred much lower costs than implied by the April index, meaning MCO could show a larger cost increase than the farm actually experienced. Diesel can create a different timing mismatch because a substantial share of fuel use may occur later in the crop year, after the April MCO price period.

      The relationship between the insured cost index and actual farm costs is therefore specific to the crop and operation. This does not eliminate the value of cost-sensitive coverage, but it affects how closely an indemnity tracks the producer's realized margin loss. Producers evaluating MCO should consider cost basis risk alongside county yield basis risk and the product's ability to respond to broader movements in fertilizer and energy prices. The 2026 shock is particularly useful in this regard because it provides the first opportunity to observe how the MCO index behaves during a large and sudden increase in selected input costs.

      What 2026 Could Mean for 2027

      The first year of MCO gives producers a concrete example of the type of risk the product was designed to cover. A geopolitical disruption sharply increased fertilizer and energy prices, increasing projected MCO payments all else equal. On the other hand, higher crop futures prices in the fall might offer producers an opportunity to lock in a high projected price. That experience could influence future enrollment, particularly among producers who view fertilizer and energy price volatility as an important source of farm-level risk. It does not, however, make the choice between MCO and other supplemental products straightforward because the product must be evaluated before the next shock is known.

      The most important competitive constraint remains ECO. Because their coverage bands overlap, producers cannot purchase both MCO and ECO, and ECO entered 2026 with a much larger enrollment base. Producers must therefore weigh MCO's explicit treatment of selected input costs against ECO's supplemental revenue protection and the basis risk embedded in county-level margins. Timing also matters because producers made their 2026 MCO decisions the previous fall, before the Hormuz disruption was known. Those who did not purchase MCO could not add coverage after input prices began to rise, so the product protects against an uncertain future margin shock rather than allowing producers to insure a shock after it appears.

      The level of input prices during the August to September 2026 discovery period will also shape the 2027 outlook. If fertilizer and energy prices remain elevated, the 2027 MCO projected-cost index will begin from a higher base, reducing the magnitude of another increase unless prices rise further by April. If input prices normalize before the fall discovery period, the projected index will reset lower and could again leave substantial exposure to a renewed price spike during the crop year. Finally, coverage band changes for crop year 2027 will also affect MCO. For crop year 2027, MCO will carry a coverage band comparable to ECO, covering county margins from 90 to 95 percent. Essentially, MCO-90 is eliminated and MCO-95 has a reduced coverage band.

      Future adoption will therefore depend not only on the experience of 2026 but also on expectations about input markets, perceptions of basis risk, changes to producer premiums, and how producers value MCO relative to ECO.

      The Broader Lesson

      MCO remains a small part of the crop insurance portfolio, but its first year has provided a clear demonstration of what margin coverage can add. The 2026 Hormuz disruption affected farms primarily through fertilizer and energy costs rather than through grain prices, exposing a risk that traditional revenue coverage does not directly address. For the relatively small group of producers who entered 2026 with MCO-95, current conditions imply elevated probabilities of payment and positive expected net returns. Actual indemnities will not be known until harvest crop prices and county yields are finalized, and farm-level outcomes can differ substantially from the county index. Even with those qualifications, the episode shows why the cost side of the margin can matter for crop insurance design.

      The broader lesson extends beyond the final size of 2026 MCO payments. Geopolitical shocks can reach farm profitability quickly through production costs, and those shocks need not be accompanied by higher crop prices that offset the increase in expenses. MCO provides one mechanism for insuring part of that exposure while retaining the limitations of an area-based index product. The 2026 crop year therefore offers the first real-world test of whether margin-based supplemental coverage can fill a meaningful gap in the existing crop insurance portfolio.

      Conclusion

      Supplemental crop insurance products were designed to address a well-known limitation of traditional federal crop insurance by covering “shallow losses” that occur within policy deductibles but can nevertheless have meaningful effects on farm income. Despite this objective and relatively high premium subsidies since their introduction in the 2014 Farm Bill, adoption of supplemental products remained limited through 2024. Program complexity, restrictive eligibility rules, concerns about basis risk associated with area-based triggers, and limited familiarity among producers and agents all contributed to historically low participation.

      OBBBA represents a major shift in supplemental insurance policy intended to reduce some of these barriers. By increasing premium subsidies across major supplemental products, removing longstanding coordination constraints with ARC/PLC elections, expanding allowable coverage levels, and increasing premium-subsidy support for Beginning Farmers and Ranchers, the Act alters the cost-benefit tradeoffs facing producers. The sharp increase in ECO participation in 2025 following the subsidy increase is consistent with demand for shallow-loss coverage being responsive to lower out-of-pocket cost. Early 2026 policy sales point to substantial expansion: the projections put ECO at 61.8 percent of eligible acreage and SCO at 26.6 percent, multiplying their 2025 rates by about 2.3 and 5.7, respectively. The SCO response is the more striking of the two, because SCO had been contracting rather than growing: after its 2023 high of 6.79 percent of eligible acreage, adoption had slipped to 4.69 percent by 2025, and the projected reversal coincides with a year in which OBBBA both raised the SCO subsidy from 65 to 80 percent and removed the ARC election constraint. The data do not separate these. In the cells where the acreage-reporting window has already closed, observed ECO participation sits about 10 percentage points below the projection, so these remain early signals rather than realized outcomes.

      At the same time, the analysis shows that acreage participation and insured value grow at very different rates. Even when adoption expands substantially, supplemental products still cover narrow slices of loss above the underlying policy, and how much insured value an enrolled acre adds depends on the region and on the underlying coverage level the producer elects. In particular, under the 2027 program design ECO covers only the 90 to 95 percent band, the slice of the deductible that pays out most often relative to the deeper SCO layer beneath it. Concentrating subsidy-supported demand in the band most likely to pay is consistent with optimal choice when producers face a premium budget, but the structural implication remains that large increases in insured acres may translate into only modest increases in insured production value while meaningful exposure to moderate losses can persist if band concentration continues. These findings suggest that supplemental insurance under OBBBA deepens protection at the margin rather than fundamentally closing the shallow-loss gap.

      The report also shows that the effects of OBBBA differ between the 2026 transition year and the 2027 program design. In 2026, higher subsidies are applied largely to the pre-OBBBA coverage structure. By contrast, the 2027 design moves both levers at once: subsidies rise, and the recalibrated SCO and ECO bands rework what the products charge and what they pay. Accordingly, the participation and net-benefit improvements recorded in the 2026 transition year do not map directly onto the settled 2027 program, and part of that improvement recedes once the revised structure takes effect.

      The featured article adds a distinct lesson. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption raised fertilizer and diesel costs through the Margin Coverage Option's April price discovery window. Margin-based coverage can therefore respond to cost shocks that revenue-based supplemental products are not structured to address. Its reach remains small, at 8,959 policies nationally, largely because MCO and ECO cannot be combined and so compete for the same enrollment decision.

      Several factors will shape how these policy changes ultimately affect producer outcomes. Basis risk will likely continue to limit the attractiveness of area-based coverage in heterogeneous production environments, and interactions between supplemental and individual coverage decisions may generate substitution effects not fully captured in the present analysis. In addition, the fiscal and risk-distribution consequences of expanded supplemental coverage will depend on realized indemnities, future rate adjustments, and the geographic concentration of participation. Subsequent monitoring of enrollment, premium expenditures, and loss experience as OBBBA's 2026 transition year gives way to the 2027 program design will be needed to assess how the expanded supplemental framework affects farm income variability and program cost over time.

      The estimates and analytical framework presented in this report should be interpreted as an early baseline for evaluating OBBBA's supplemental provisions as additional enrollment and indemnity data become available. The Agricultural Risk Policy Center (ARPC) is developing a broader simulation framework to support that work and to provide a more comprehensive assessment of how OBBBA may reshape supplemental crop insurance participation in the years ahead. Future work can build on this baseline by examining fiscal exposure, the interaction between supplemental products and other farm safety net choices, and the distribution of supplemental participation across crops, farm types, and regions.

      Appendix A: Recalibrating Supplemental Area-Plan Rates to Alternative Coverage Bands

      Recent provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) modify the coverage structure of supplemental area-based crop insurance beginning in the 2027 crop year. The Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) upper trigger increases from 86 to 90 percent, while the Enhanced Coverage Option (ECO) coverage band narrows from 86–95 percent to 90–95 percent. Because official premium parameters reflecting these changes will not appear in the Risk Management Agency (RMA) Actuarial Data Master (ADM) until late 2026 or early 2027, a temporary gap exists for policy analysis. This technical note presents a transparent method for approximating revised premium parameters by scaling observed ADM base rates and payment factors according to changes in insured band width. Historical recalibrated rates for the OBBBA-adjusted coverage bands for crop years 2015–2026 are the inputs to the retrospective simulation reported in the Outlook section; they are produced by applying the procedure described below to the published ADM and are released as an accompanying ARPC data file.

      Policy Motivation for Rate Recalibration

      Although the 2027 band changes described earlier in this report will apply starting in the 2027 crop year, the official premium parameters reflecting the new band structures will not appear in the RMA ADM until late in the 2026 rating cycle or early in 2027. As a result, analysts seeking to evaluate the policy implications of the OBBBA reforms must conduct analysis using ADM data that still reflect the historical coverage bands.

      This creates a practical challenge for policy simulation, outlook analysis, and program evaluation. To address this timing gap, it is useful to construct an approximate recalibration of the observed premium parameters so that they reflect the modified coverage intervals implied by the new legislation.

      Such a recalibration allows analysts to simulate producer incentives, premium costs, subsidy flows, and expected indemnities under the revised program structure using currently available data. While this approach does not replace the official actuarial rating process conducted by RMA, it provides a transparent and analytically consistent approximation that is sufficient for forward-looking policy analysis.

      Relationship Between Coverage Band and Premium

      Let the original insured coverage band be defined by two parameters: \(S\), the area loss start percent (upper trigger), and \(E\), the area loss end percent (lower trigger). The width of the original insured band is

      \[ B_old = S - E. \]

      This quantity represents the interval of losses over which indemnities may occur under the original policy structure.

      The calibration method described in this note is based on the observation that the premium components of supplemental area plans are closely related to the width of the insured coverage band. When the insured interval expands, a larger range of potential losses becomes indemnifiable. This increases expected payouts and therefore the appropriate premium level.

      Conversely, when the band narrows, the range of covered losses decreases. This reduces expected indemnities and lowers the premium. This relationship suggests that, as a first-order approximation, the premium parameters can be scaled in proportion to the change in band width.

      Recalibration of Premium and Payment Parameters Under Modified Coverage Bands

      Building on the band-width relationship described in the preceding subsection, suppose a policy change modifies one or both endpoints of the insured band. Let \(_S\) denote the adjustment applied to the start percent and \(_E\) denote the adjustment applied to the end percent. The modified endpoints become

      \[ S^* = S + _S      and      E^* = E + _E. \]

      The width of the modified band is therefore

      \[ B_new = S^* - E^* = (S + _S) - (E + _E). \]

      Because official actuarial parameters for modified coverage structures may not yet exist, we approximate the effect of the band change using several complementary calibration approaches. Each method constructs a differential that translates observed actuarial parameters from the original band to the modified band.

      Band-Width Proportional Calibration

      The simplest calibration assumes that expected loss costs scale proportionally with the width of the insured band. Under this approximation, the rate adjustment factor is defined as

      \[ D = B_newB_old. \]

      Substituting the band definitions yields

      \[ D = (S + _S) - (E + _E)S - E. \]

      This factor represents the proportional change in insured band width between the modified and original coverage structures. If the new band is wider than the original band, the factor exceeds one; if the new band is narrower, the factor is less than one.

      Because extremely small original band widths can produce unstable scaling factors, a stability adjustment is applied before the differential is used to recalibrate premium components. When the original band width is very small, the recalibration factor can become extremely large. For example, if

      \[ B_old = 0.02      and      B_new = 0.08, \]

      then

      \[ D = 4. \]

      Such extreme adjustments typically arise from very small denominators rather than meaningful differences in actuarial risk. To prevent unstable scaling, the recalibration factor is capped at an upper bound such that

      \[ D^* = (D, 2). \]

      This cap limits the maximum upward adjustment to a doubling of the original premium components while preserving proportional relationships for typical band widths.

      Let \(R\) denote the observed base rate associated with the original coverage band. The recalibrated base rate for the modified band is computed as

      \[ R^* = R D^*. \]

      Similarly, if \(P\) denotes the observed payment factor under the original band, the recalibrated payment factor is

      \[ P^* = P D^*. \]

      Applying the same adjustment factor to both premium components maintains internal consistency between rate parameters.

      In practice, rating data may contain multiple observations within a geographic and commodity grouping. Let \(D_i\) denote the recalibration factor computed for record \(i\) within a given group. If there are \(n\) observations within that group, the average calibration factor is

      \[ D = 1n _i=1^n D_i. \]

      This averaged factor provides a stable calibration multiplier that can then be applied to detailed rate records within the same group.

      Structural Rate Calibration Using ADM Relationships

      While proportional band-width scaling provides a simple approximation, actuarial rates in the Federal Crop Insurance Program (FCIP) also depend on the position of the band within the loss distribution and on plan-specific design features. To capture these structural relationships, we estimate an empirical model linking observed base rates to key band parameters using data from the ADM.

      Within each geographic and commodity grouping, we estimate the log-linear relationship

      \[ (R) = _0 + _1 (B) + _2 (E) + _3 RP + _4 RP_HPE. \]

      Here, \(R\) is the observed base rate, \(B\) is the coverage band width, \(E\) is the lower endpoint of the band, and \(RP\) and \(RP_HPE\) are indicator variables for revenue protection plan variants. Using the estimated coefficients, predicted base rates are computed for both the original band and the modified band:

      \[ R_old      and      R_new. \]

      The implied regression-based calibration factor is

      \[ D_reg = R_newR_old. \]

      This approach preserves the empirical relationships embedded in ADM rate construction and allows the calibration to reflect how actuarial rates vary with both band width and band position.

      Empirical Loss-Cost Calibration Using Historical Yield Outcomes

      A third calibration method uses historical yield outcomes to approximate how expected indemnities would change under the modified coverage band. Historical observations of expected and realized yields are combined with the FCIP payment formula to simulate payment rates under both the original and modified band definitions.

      For each observation, payment rates are computed using the original coverage band and the modified coverage band. Expected payment rates are then averaged within each geographic grouping to obtain

      \[ E [payment rate_old]      and      E [payment rate_new]. \]

      The empirical loss-cost differential is defined as

      \[ D_emp = E [payment rate_new] E [payment rate_old]. \]

      To account for alternative treatments of yield trends, this simulation procedure is implemented using three yield measures: observed yields, trended yields, and detrended yields. These alternatives produce three empirical calibration factors that reflect how expected indemnities would have changed if the modified coverage band had historically been in place.

      Payment Differential Calibration

      Finally, payment differentials are computed directly from the FCIP payment formula using ADM price and index data. Using observed index values and price parameters, payment rates are simulated under both the original and modified band definitions while holding other contract parameters fixed.

      Let \(Q_old\) denote the payment rate computed under the original band and \(Q_new\) the payment rate under the modified band. The resulting payment differential is

      \[ D_pay = Q_newQ_old. \]

      This differential isolates the direct effect of the band modification on indemnity payments and provides an additional benchmark for evaluating the magnitude of the policy change.

      Interpretation and Conclusion

      Across these calibration methods, the differential has a consistent interpretation. If the differential exceeds one, the modified band implies greater expected indemnity exposure and higher actuarial rates. If the differential is less than one, the modified band reduces expected exposure and actuarial rates decline proportionally. When the differential equals one, the modified and original band structures imply identical expected loss exposure.

      The proportional band-width calibration described in this report provides a simple and transparent method for approximating supplemental area-plan premium parameters under modified coverage structures. Rescaling the published rate and payment parameters in proportion to how much the insured band widens or narrows yields approximate premium schedules that reflect the policy changes introduced by the OBBBA.

      This approach enables timely evaluation of producer incentives, premium costs, subsidy exposure, and expected risk protection under the revised SCO and ECO structures before official actuarial parameters become available. Once the official rates reflecting the new coverage bands are published in the RMA ADM, those values can replace the calibrated approximations used in this analysis.

      For transparency and reproducibility, historical recalibrated base rates and payment factors for the OBBBA-adjusted SCO and ECO coverage bands for crop years 2015 through 2026 are maintained in a companion repository and are available on request.

      Beyond the immediate application to OBBBA reforms, this calibration framework has broader practical value for agricultural policy analysis. The method can be used to approximate premium parameters for any proposed change in supplemental coverage bands by translating existing ADM rate schedules into alternative band structures.

      This allows analysts to evaluate the potential implications of proposed policy adjustments prior to legislative or regulatory implementation. In particular, the approach enables forward-looking assessments of how changes in coverage bands may affect producer risk protection, expected indemnity exposure, premium costs, subsidy levels, and the overall actuarial performance of the crop insurance program.

      Because the method relies only on currently available ADM rating parameters and a transparent proportional adjustment based on band width, it can be readily incorporated into simulation models and policy evaluation frameworks. As a result, the calibration approach provides a practical tool for evaluating potential program design changes, supporting scenario analysis, and informing policy discussions regarding the structure, performance, and fiscal implications of supplemental crop insurance products.

      Appendix B: Featured Article Supplementary Exhibits

      Three exhibits set out the mechanism behind the featured article: when the cost shock could reach the insured margin, how it was converted into an indexed cost, and who was exposed when it did.

      Timing comes first. Figure 21 illustrates the typical MCO price discovery timeline for corn in most states. Projected input and crop prices are set in the fall before the insured crop year, final input prices are set in April, and final crop prices follow the harvest discovery period. That sequencing is what allowed the 2026 cost shock to enter the insured margin after enrollment had closed, leaving enrolled producers holding a contract whose cost side moved underneath them.

      Supplementary Note: Simulation Approach

      A simulation approach is used to derive expected payments for MCO-95 for corn and soybeans. The process begins by using futures prices (December contracts for corn and November contracts for soybeans) and implied volatilities at expiration, adjusted to October, to estimate a lognormal distribution of crop harvest prices. The corn December contract is $5.34 per bushel and the soybean November contract is $13.32 per bushel. Implied volatilities are 10.5 percent and 7.1 percent at expiration, respectively.

      Average county yields are assumed to equal RMA expected yields. Historical RMA county yields for non-irrigated practices from 1995 to 2024 are detrended using a linear trend and expressed in 2026 values, after which the standard deviation is computed. A Weibull distribution is then fitted for each county by the method of moments, using the county-specific mean and standard deviation as inputs.

      Because MCO is evaluated in combination with Revenue Protection, farm-level yields are simulated alongside county yields. Farm expected yield is set equal to the county expected yield, farm yield standard deviation is set 25 percent above the county standard deviation to reflect the greater dispersion of individual yields relative to a county average, and the correlation between farm and county yields is set at 0.7. These three parameters are assumptions rather than estimates, and the farm-level results are correspondingly less precisely identified than the county-level ones.

      Finally, using state-level yield-price correlations from RMA's COMBO rating methodology, a normal copula is generated using the Iman and Conover method (Iman and Conover, 1982) to jointly model yields and prices. This imposes the historical correlation structure between the two variables, which is negative in most Midwest states.

      Based on 10,000 simulated county yields and harvest prices, indemnities are calculated for MCO with a 95 percent coverage band when purchased in combination with Revenue Protection. Following the Revenue Protection provisions, the harvest price entering the revenue guarantee is floored at the projected price and capped at twice it. Producer-paid premium is computed from the MCO-95 base rate applied to liability, net of the 80 percent federal subsidy that applies to the endorsement, so the expected net returns reported above are net of the subsidized premium rather than the gross premium.

      Appendix C: Validating the Early Adoption Projection Against Reported Acreage

      The projection above assumes that acres per policy in 2026 hold at recent historical levels. That assumption is now partly testable. Acreage reporting has closed for 100.0 percent of the underlying insured acres in the counties and commodities considered in this section, and those acres are reflected in the Summary of Business as of October 15, 2026. A closed reporting deadline is not the same as every acre having been posted, which is why the projection above is still required; what it does mean is that these cells are no longer waiting on producers to file. Because underlying and supplemental acres are carried on the same acreage report, any remaining reporting lag scales the numerator and the denominator of the adoption rate in common and therefore largely cancels, so adoption observed in these cells is a considerably firmer quantity than the acreage levels themselves.

      Table 7 compares projected and observed adoption for exactly this set of cells. Observed Enhanced Coverage Option (ECO) adoption is 9.9 percentage points below the projection, and observed Supplemental Coverage Option (SCO) adoption is 2.7 percentage points above it. The acres-per-policy columns locate the source of any divergence: where observed acres per policy exceed the assumed value, the projection understates eventual adoption, and where they fall short of it, the projection overstates it.

      About the authors

      Francis Tsiboe, Ph.D.

      Dr. Francis Tsiboe is a Senior Research Economist and Program Leader with the Agricultural Risk Policy Center at North Dakota State University. His work focuses on risk management strategies and agricultural policy, with particular emphasis on how farm-level risk and insurance programs affect U.S. agricultural producers.

      Henrique Monaco, Ph.D.

      Dr. Henrique Monaco is an Assistant Professor at the University of Minnesota. His work focuses on agricultural finance, farm management, crop insurance, and risk management, using quantitative methods to study financial decision-making by farmers and its implications for commodity markets and policy design.

      Hongxi Zhao, Ph.D.

      Dr. Hongxi Zhao is a Junior Research Economist with the Agricultural Risk Policy Center at North Dakota State University. Her research focuses on efficient land use and outcomes across the urban-rural spectrum, relying on regional and environmental modeling, econometric methods, and non-market valuation.

      Jennifer Ifft, Ph.D.

      Dr. Jennifer Ifft is a Professor and Extension Specialist in Agricultural Policy at Kansas State University. Her research and extension program covers policy issues affecting the viability of U.S. and Kansas agriculture, with current work on nontraditional finance, crop insurance, farmland markets, and farm labor.

      Rwit Chakravorty, Ph.D.

      Dr. Rwit Chakravorty is a Junior Research Economist with the Agricultural Risk Policy Center at North Dakota State University. His research focuses on agricultural production economics, risk management, and market disruptions influencing input costs in domestic and global markets.

      Dylan Turner, Ph.D.

      Dr. Dylan Turner is a Senior Research Economist with the Agricultural Risk Policy Center at North Dakota State University. His work focuses on agricultural policy, risk management, decision-making under uncertainty, and natural hazards, analyzing how risk and insurance markets affect producers and the broader agricultural sector.

      Shawn Arita, Ph.D.

      Dr. Shawn Arita is the Associate Director of the Agricultural Risk Policy Center at North Dakota State University. His work focuses on agricultural policy, commodity markets, and trade-related risk, using economic modeling and impact assessment to understand how global markets and policy changes affect U.S. producers.
